implementation_notes: Language-integrated query is the C# realisation of the pattern: System.Linq.Enumerable extension methods are lazy (deferred execution) and compose over any IEnumerable<T>, while the sink is chosen separately - foreach, ToList/ToArray, Aggregate, Sum, a Channel writer or another query. Custom transformations are ordinary iterator methods (yield return) or extension methods over IEnumerable<T>, and query syntax (from ... where ... select) is sugar over the same operators, so the pipeline reads declaratively and still composes as values. What replaces the classic structure: no reducing-function transformer object is needed - the accumulator is supplied at the terminal (Aggregate, Sum, ToDictionary) and the pipeline is the composition of static generic methods. The classic transducer shape is still worth writing when the transformation must be exposed as a single value of one type (Func<IEnumerable<T>, IEnumerable<R>>) or must feed a sink that is not an IEnumerable.
code_sketch:
IEnumerable<Reading> Pipeline(IEnumerable<Reading> src) =>
    src.Where(r => r.IsValid)
       .Select(r => r with { Value = r.Value * Scale })
       .Take(100);                                 // nothing runs yet
var total = Pipeline(Readings()).Sum(r => r.Value);      // terminal drives it
foreach (var g in Pipeline(Readings()).GroupBy(r => r.Sensor)) { ... }   // same query, new sink
pitfalls: Deferred execution re-runs the query on every enumeration and captures variables at execution time, so a mutated captured variable or a disposed source changes the result of a query that looked already computed.
Enumerating the same query twice (Count() then foreach) doubles the work; materialise once (ToList) when the result is used more than once.
Mixing IQueryable (EF Core/ORMs) with Enumerable operators silently switches to client-side evaluation and materialises the whole table - keep the provider's operators until the terminal.

variants.name: Async LINQ over IAsyncEnumerable<T>
variants.implementation_notes: C# 8 async streams move the same operator vocabulary to asynchronous sources: IAsyncEnumerable<T> with await foreach, and since .NET 10 the operators ship in the base class library as System.Linq.AsyncEnumerable (before that the community System.Linq.Async package; the two are ambiguous side by side and Ix.NET v7 now deprecates its own). Sources are anything producing values asynchronously - Channel readers, sockets, EF Core's AsAsyncEnumerable - and the sink is an async terminal (await foreach, ToListAsync, AggregateAsync, SumAsync), with a CancellationToken threaded through every step so cancellation propagates with the pipeline. What replaces the classic structure: as in the synchronous case, static generic extension methods plus a terminal, with pull-based await instead of a transducer's step/completion protocol; the classic form is needed only for a pipeline that must be stored as one type across both worlds.
variants.code_sketch:
IAsyncEnumerable<double> Values(IAsyncEnumerable<Reading> src, CancellationToken ct) =>
    src.Where(r => r.IsValid)
       .Select(r => r.Value * Scale)
       .Take(100);                                    // still nothing runs

await foreach (var v in Values(Readings(ct), ct).WithCancellation(ct))
    Use(v);
var sum = await Values(Readings(ct), ct).SumAsync(ct);   // .NET 10 System.Linq.AsyncEnumerable
pitfalls: Async LINQ requires await foreach / async terminals; blocking with .Result or .Wait() on an async sequence deadlocks under a synchronisation context and defeats cancellation.

The operator surfaces differ by provider - .NET 10's System.Linq.AsyncEnumerable, Ix.NET's System.Linq.Async and EF Core's AsAsyncEnumerable overlap - and referencing two of them produces CS0121 ambiguous-call errors.
Cancellation only works when the token is threaded into every step and the source honours it; a pipeline that ignores ct keeps consuming after the caller gave up.
